title: Rank Bottlenecks in Link Prediction
one_liner: Neural networks that predict links in graphs hit a mathematical ceiling when they squeeze information through a narrow passage, and non-linear layers break the ceiling.
lead: Link prediction models learn to guess which entities should connect in a graph. They compress entities into a small list of numbers, then re-expand that list to make predictions. When the graph is huge and densely connected, the expansion bottleneck becomes a mathematical limit — some functions become impossible to represent no matter how you train. This paper proves exactly how tight that ceiling is, then shows how non-linear layers can shatter it.

paras: Link prediction models predict which pairs of things should be connected in a graph. Start with entities (nodes): users, movies, or proteins. The model learns a short list of numbers for each entity — its embedding (a compressed summary). To predict a link, the model re-expands each embedding using a linear layer (a simple transformation that multiplies the embedding by a grid of learned numbers) to score all possible connections. This works fine at small scale. But graphs in the real world are huge: millions of entities, billions of potential edges. The linear layer is doing something impossible: it needs to capture all the nuances of connection rules using a thin pipeline.

A beginner might think: scale up the embedding size. But that is expensive — more memory, slower training. The paper shows this is not even the core problem. The core is that a linear output layer has a hard mathematical limit on what functions it can represent. Some link patterns become impossible to learn no matter how big the embedding is, if you use only linear layers. That is the rank bottleneck: a bottleneck is a narrow passage that chokes flow; here, information about entities is squeezed through too narrow a rank space.

callout.html: Linear layers in link prediction models hit a mathematical ceiling that grows with graph size — they cannot represent all the functions needed to predict links correctly.

steps.text: For any link prediction model with a linear output layer, the paper derives a necessary lower bound on embedding size that grows with graph size and edge density.
The paper proves that some link patterns become mathematically impossible to express if embedding size is below this bound.
Using a mixture model (a gated combination of multiple non-linear paths), add expressive power without huge tuned-weight overhead.
Test on large, dense knowledge graphs and show the non-linear layer recovers functions the linear layer cannot learn.

The non-linear model matches link predictions better because the mixture lets different link patterns route through different experts instead of colliding in one narrow rank space. It adds only modest tuned weights because each expert is small.

paras: The output layer: replacing a single linear transformation with a non-linear mixture model that routes different entity pairs through different learned pathways.

hidden.name: matrix rank (the true expressive ceiling)
paras: Rank is a number that tells you how many independent directions a matrix can represent. If a matrix has rank 64, it can only express patterns along 64 independent directions. All link prediction functions must fit into this 64-dimensional space if the output layer is linear. When graph size grows, the number of different link patterns needed explodes, but rank stays fixed. At some point, patterns collide: you cannot fit the function, no matter how training nudges the weights.

The paper calculates the minimum rank needed to represent all link-prediction functions for a given graph. It then shows that a linear layer cannot achieve this rank when the graph is large and dense. The non-linear mixture layer increases effective rank by routing entity pairs along different learned paths, each with its own linear transformation.

heat.caption: Darker means higher rank (more expressive power). Large dense graphs need very high rank.

reads.html: Rank is how many independent directions a matrix can encode. A rank-64 matrix can only express 64 different patterns, no matter how many entity pairs you have.

The rank of the output layer is bounded by the embedding dimension. For a graph with N entities, the paper proves necessary rank grows with N and graph density, but linear layers stay rank-constrained.

mechanism.h2: Why non-linear layers break the ceiling
paras: A linear layer multiplies the embedding by a fixed matrix. This matrix has rank at most 64 (the embedding size). No matter how many tuned weights the matrix has, it cannot express patterns that need rank higher than 64. The paper proves: for large dense graphs, you need rank much higher than 64 to fit all link rules. So linear layers fail.

A non-linear mixture model works differently. It learns a gating function (a trained router) that looks at each entity pair and decides which of multiple learned experts to use. Each expert is a small linear transformation. By switching between experts, the effective rank becomes much higher — you can now express patterns that were forbidden before. Adding non-linearity (the routing decision) increases the effective rank of the model without scaling tuned weights linearly with graph size. The mixture adds expressive power efficiently because each expert is small.

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Graph with 10000 entities, density 0.01 (1 percent of edges exist).
Minimum rank needed = roughly 10000 times square root of 0.01 = 10000 times 0.1 = 1000.
Linear layer with 64-dimensional embeddings has rank at most 64.
Rank gap = 1000 divided by 64 = 15.6x more expressive power needed than linear layers provide.
Non-linear mixture with multiple experts can increase effective rank to match.
Without non-linearity, 1000 dimension embeddings would be needed — far more expensive.

math.note: The rank ceiling grows with graph size but non-linear routing breaks it without matching tuned-weight cost.

items.html: The gating function might route everything to one expert, wasting the mixture. This happens if training does not push experts toward specialization.
Non-linear routing adds degrees of freedom. If training data is sparse relative to graph size, the model may memorize spurious patterns instead of learning generalizable link rules.
The theory tells you minimum rank based on known density, but in practice density might vary across subgraphs or change as the graph grows. The fixed-rank design might be wrong halfway through.

Gently steer the router to spread load evenly across experts by adding a penalty for unbalanced routing; validate on edges held back during training; and retrain periodically if the graph topology shifts.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small knowledge graph with 1000 entities and 0.5 percent density. Generate synthetic link patterns that require high rank to represent (e.g., hierarchical transitivity where ancestor-of-ancestor-of-X rules apply). Train a link prediction model with a linear output layer on this graph and measure ranking accuracy. The accuracy should plateau well below 100 percent because the linear layer cannot express the high-rank patterns. Then train the same model with a non-linear mixture output layer using multiple experts and gated routing, and measure again. The non-linear version should break the plateau and recover higher accuracy, proving that the rank bottleneck was real and that the non-linear routing can break it by letting different patterns flow through different experts.
demo.closing: If improvement is zero or tiny, the synthetic patterns do not exercise rank-limited functions. Redesign the pattern generator. If improvement is large, the rank bottleneck hypothesis is confirmed on this graph.
